Software Engineering team project — living decision history

Every codebase remembers what it does. Ours remembers why.

Repositories preserve what a team built, but the reasoning disappears — the rejected alternatives, the evidence, the argument that settled it. Context Engine reconstructs that history from your commits, issues, discussions, and docs, and keeps it alive as the project evolves.

the problem

You can read the code. You can't read the reasoning.

Our primary user is a developer joining or taking over an existing project — a 5–30 person student, startup, open-source, or product team. They can see what the system does. They can't see why it was built that way.

What the repository tells you

  • What the system currently does
  • Which files changed, and when
  • Who touched which lines
  • The current architecture, as it stands today

What it doesn't tell you

  • Why important decisions were made
  • What alternatives were considered and rejected
  • What evidence led to the current implementation
  • Whether the reasoning still holds today

"When developers join or revisit an existing project, the repository tells them what the system does, but not reliably why decisions were made, what alternatives were rejected, or what evidence led to the current implementation."

isn't this already
solved?

Several tools solve parts of this. Our contribution is the missing combination: a time-aware history that connects discussions → decisions → experiments → code changes → current implementation, with the evidence and every later change kept attached to it.

not another enterprise search engine
the pipeline

From scattered sources to a single, queryable history

Four channels feed a pipeline that turns raw activity into a structured, evidence-backed timeline — surfaced through one hosted web interface.

Git
GitHub
Docs
Slack
1

Ingestion

Pulls commits, PRs, issues, threads, and documents into one intake layer.

2

Entity extraction

Identifies the people, components, and artifacts each piece of activity refers to.

3

Event linking

Connects related activity across tools into a single thread of reasoning.

4

Temporal graph

Orders linked events in time, so later decisions stay attached to earlier ones.

5

Decision engine

Distinguishes discussion from a decision, and a decision from a rejected alternative.

6

Evidence retrieval

Surfaces the experiment results and threads that justified each decision.

7

LLM

Turns the retrieved evidence into a plain-language answer, not just a list of links.

8

Web interface

One hosted app — developers work with repositories and docs, not a phone.

the timeline

How one decision becomes "current implementation"

This is the lifecycle Context Engine reconstructs for every decision in a project — and keeps extending as the project moves forward.

01

Event

Something happens that needs a response — a bug, a new requirement, a limit the team hits.

02

Discussion

The team weighs options across issues, PRs, docs, and chat — often in more than one place at once.

03

Decision

An option is chosen. Context Engine records what was chosen, what wasn't, and why.

04

Experiment

The decision is tested — a spike, a staging run, a benchmark — and the result is attached as evidence.

05

Code change

The decision ships. The commit or PR is linked back to the discussion that produced it.

06

Later decision

Circumstances change and the team revisits the choice — the new decision links to the old one instead of replacing it.

07

Current implementation

What's live today, with a full chain back to the event that started it — the "why" a new developer actually needs.

killer feature

Onboarding mode

New developers don't need ten thousand documents dumped on them. They need an answer that starts broad and lets them drill down.

"I'm new to this project."

One prompt opens a guided chain — each step answerable on its own, and each one linking to the evidence behind it.

evaluation

Measured against how teams already try to solve this

We're not claiming this problem is unsolved — we're claiming the usual answers are incomplete. Three baselines make that case.

baseline 01

Repository & doc search

Finds the file. Doesn't explain why it looks the way it does, or what was tried before it.

baseline 02

Copilot / codebase Q&A

Answers a question when it's asked, from the code as it exists now — with no persistent memory of the reasoning behind it.

baseline 03

Manual ADRs

Architecture Decision Records work when someone remembers to write them — and stop working the moment someone doesn't.
